# Overview

Cell type labels in spatial single-cell data are rarely certain: transcripts leak between neighbouring cells and each cell has few counts, so closely related subtypes such as CD4+ and CD8+ T cells are easily confused. Yet most analyses treat every label as known, and that uncertainty flows unseen into cell type proportions, co-localisation and niches.

*fuzzyCell* measures it. For each group of closely related subtypes, it resamples every cell's transcript counts and re-classifies the cell. The fraction of resamples in which the cell lands in a subtype is its **confidence** in that subtype. These confidences act as **soft cell type weights**, so a cell can count towards several subtypes instead of one. Every analysis can be run with the original labels (*unweighted*) and with the weights (*weighted*), and comparing the two shows which conclusions depend on uncertain labels.

| If you want to know... | Use | Built on |
|:-------------------------------------|:----------------|:----------------|
| whether a cell type's proportion differs between outcomes | `runProportionsPipeline()`, `runProportionsRelativeToParentPipeline()` | linear models of image-level proportions |
| whether two cell types co-localise more or less between outcomes | `runColocalisationModels()` | [spicyR](https://bioconductor.org/packages/spicyR)'s L-function, and Statial's Kontextual test for relative co-localisation |
| whether tissue neighbourhoods (niches) differ between outcomes | `runNicheIdentification()`, `testNicheOutcome()` | [lisaClust](https://bioconductor.org/packages/lisaClust) |

The rest of this vignette follows the workflow on a real dataset.

# Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("fuzzyCell")
```

::: callout-note
fuzzyCell builds on recent versions of spicyR (\>= 1.99.32) and lisaClust (\>= 1.21.9), which come with Bioconductor 3.24 and later.
:::

# Example data: lung biopsies

We follow the whole workflow on Xenium lung biopsies from patients with pulmonary fibrosis and from controls (Vannan et al., 2025). The full data are available as `SpatialDatasets::spe_Vannan_2025()`. The package includes a small subset, `lungSubset`: five control and five disease biopsies, each cropped to a window of about 3,000 cells at its centre. Every image comes from a different patient, and `disease_status` records whether the patient is a control or has pulmonary fibrosis.

```{r data}
library(fuzzyCell)
library(SpatialExperiment)
library(ggplot2)

data(lungSubset)
spe = lungSubset
spe

# one image (and one outcome) per patient
imageOutcome = unique(colData(spe)[, c("imageID", "disease_status")])
table(imageOutcome$disease_status)
```

::: callout-note
The subset is for illustration only. With five images per group, which cell types differ between the outcomes depends on which biopsies and windows were chosen.
:::

::: callout-note
Any `SummarizedExperiment` (such as a `SpatialExperiment`) works as long as it has a `"counts"` assay and the cell metadata columns `cellID`, `imageID`, `cellType`, `x` and `y` in its `colData`. If your columns are named differently, the analysis functions take arguments (such as `cellType` and `imageID`) giving the column names.
:::

# The cell type tree

Confidence is calculated between closely related cell types, so fuzzyCell needs to know which those are. You describe them in a nested list: a group of subtypes that should be refined together is written `list(children = ...)`, and everything else is either organisational nesting (a lineage such as `"Immune"`) or a plain leaf cell type (such as `"SMCs/Pericytes"`). The tree for the lung data is included in the package. Here is its mesenchymal branch, and the groups it defines:

```{r tree}
data(lungCellTypeTree)
tree = lungCellTypeTree
str(tree[["Mesenchymal"]])
buildCellTypeMap(tree)$groupsWithChildren
```

Each of these groups can get confidence scores. Cell types outside a group, such as `SMCs/Pericytes` and `Mesothelial`, are not refined and keep their hard labels.

# Bootstrap confidence

`bootstrapLineageConfidence()` does the work, group by group, as described in the Overview. Within each group it uses ridge multinomial logistic regression on the first 50 principal components of the group's cells (`classifier = "pcaLogistic"`, the default, and what we use here). `"logistic"` fits it on all genes, and `"rf"`, `"lda"` and `"svm"` are also available.

The classifier is trained with the same number of cells of each subtype, which gives every subtype the same prior. `priors = "observed"` instead weights each subtype by its share of the group's cells, so a cell is not drawn towards a rare subtype only because the subtypes were balanced in training.

We use 20 resamples to keep the vignette quick, but we encourage at least 100 for your own analysis.

```{r bootstrap, results = "hide"}
confList = bootstrapLineageConfidence(spe, tree, nBoot = 20, classifier = "pcaLogistic",
    seed = 1)
```

The result, `confList`, is a list with one data frame per group. Each data frame has one row per cell in the group, a `cellID` column, and one column per subtype holding that cell's confidence in it (between 0 and 1, adding up to 1 across the subtypes):

```{r confhead}
names(confList)
head(confList[["Endothelial lineage"]])
```

The NK lineage is missing: only one of its subtypes is in this subset, so there is nothing to choose between.

How spread out are the confidences? Here are the scores for the subtypes of two groups, the B lineage and the endothelial cells.

```{r confplot, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 6, fig.alt = "Histograms of each subtype's confidence scores, for the B lineage and the endothelial cells."}
groups = c("B lineage", "Endothelial lineage")
scores = do.call(rbind, lapply(groups, function(g) {
    conf = confList[[g]]
    do.call(rbind, lapply(setdiff(names(conf), "cellID"), function(subtype)
        data.frame(panel = paste0(g, ": ", subtype), confidence = conf[[subtype]])))
}))
ggplot(scores, aes(confidence)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#4c78a8", colour = "white") +
    facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(x = "confidence in the subtype", y = "number of cells") +
    theme_classic()
```

In the B lineage every cell scores close to 0 or 1 for each subtype, so the classifier is sure which one it is. The endothelial cells are different: many capillary cells, and some venous cells, have scores spread between 0 and 1, so they are split between subtypes. Few cells score close to 1 for arterioles, but many get a small arteriole score. Cells with scores in the middle count partly towards each subtype in the weighted analyses, which is where weighted and unweighted results can differ.

# Cell type proportions

Does the proportion of each cell type differ between controls and patients with pulmonary fibrosis? `runProportionsPipeline()` tests it with the confidences as soft counts (weighted) and with the original labels (unweighted).

```{r props, results = "hide"}
props = runProportionsPipeline(spe, tree, confList,
    outcomeCol = "disease_status", subject = "subject")
```

```{r propstables}
head(props$modelWeighted)
head(props$modelUnweighted)
```

::: callout-tip
## Reading the models

`estimate` is the difference for the *second* level of the outcome compared with the first (alphabetical order for text, factor order for factors). Here that is `Disease` minus `Control`. `p.adj` is the Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value across the cell types tested.
:::

For most cell types the weighted and unweighted analyses agree. Arterioles are one where they do not: with the original labels their proportion does not differ clearly between the outcomes, but with the confidences it is lower in disease.

```{r propscompare}
cols = c("cellType", "estimate", "p.value", "p.adj")
rbind(
    unweighted = subset(props$modelUnweighted, cellType == "Arteriole")[, cols],
    weighted = subset(props$modelWeighted, cellType == "Arteriole")[, cols])
```

`plotProportionBoxplot()` shows the per-patient proportions behind a cell type's estimate, before and after weighting. Here it is for arterioles.

```{r propsplot, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 5}
plotProportionBoxplot(props, "Arteriole", spe, "disease_status")
```

The plot is interactive: hovering over a point tells you which sample it is, so you can find the patients behind an estimate. As an example, let's look more closely at one image, the control biopsy `VUHD038`.

`plotOriginalLabelSpatial()` shows the endothelial cells of the image with their hard labels, and `plotWeightedSpatial()` shows the same cells coloured by their confidence of being arterioles.

```{r imgplots, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 6}
# the endothelial lineage with its original labels
plotOriginalLabelSpatial(spe, tree, "VUHD038", "Endothelial lineage")

# the same cells, weighted by their confidence of being arterioles
plotWeightedSpatial(spe, tree, confList, "VUHD038", "Endothelial lineage", "Arteriole")
```

Marker expression helps to judge whether the confidences are sensible. Here is the arterial marker `HEY1` in the endothelial cells of this image:

```{r imgmarkers, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 6}
plotOneMarkerSpatial(spe, "VUHD038", "Endothelial lineage", "HEY1", cellTypeTree = tree)
```

## Proportions relative to the parent group

The proportion of a subtype among all cells can change simply because its whole group changes. `runProportionsRelativeToParentPipeline()` instead measures each subtype as a proportion of its group, for example AT2 cells among all alveolar epithelial cells, and tests that in the same way.

```{r relprops, results = "hide"}
relProps = runProportionsRelativeToParentPipeline(spe, tree, confList,
    outcomeCol = "disease_status", subject = "subject")
```

AT2 cells change the most. With the original labels their share of the alveolar epithelium does not differ clearly between the outcomes; with the confidences the estimate changes direction, and it is lower in disease.

```{r relpropscompare}
rbind(
    unweighted = subset(relProps$modelUnweighted, cellType == "AT2")[, cols],
    weighted = subset(relProps$modelWeighted, cellType == "AT2")[, cols])
```

```{r relpropsplot, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 5}
plotProportionBoxplot(relProps, "AT2", spe, "disease_status")
```

# Co-localisation

Do two cell types sit closer together, or further apart, in one outcome than the other? `runColocalisationModels()` answers it for every pair of cell types and groups.

For a pair `from` → `to`, the co-localisation in an image is the cross-type L-function within 50 µm, computed by spicyR: positive when the `from` cells are attracted to the `to` cells, negative when they avoid them, and 0 for no attraction or repulsion. Each pair is then tested by a linear model of its per-image values on the outcome. With the weights, each cell contributes to a label in proportion to its confidence. *Relative* co-localisation compares a pair with the parent population of the `to` cell type, using Statial's Kontextual test with the same weights.

`confidenceWeights()` returns the weights themselves (one column per cell type and group), which you can pass to spicyR and lisaClust directly as `cellWeights`.

```{r coloc, results = "hide"}
coloc = runColocalisationModels(spe, tree, confList,
    outcomeCol = "disease_status", subject = "subject")
```

The weighted and unweighted results come back side by side. Activated fibrotic fibroblasts and SMCs/pericytes are a pair where they disagree: with the original labels their co-localisation does not differ clearly between the outcomes, while with the confidences it is lower in disease.

```{r colocresults}
subset(coloc$modelUnweighted, from == "Activated Fibrotic FBs" & to == "SMCs/Pericytes")
subset(coloc$modelWeighted, from == "Activated Fibrotic FBs" & to == "SMCs/Pericytes")
```

With `r nrow(coloc$modelWeighted)` pairs tested, though, this p-value is not significant after adjustment (`p.adj`): it is a lead to follow up rather than a finding.

`plotMetricBoxplot()` shows the per-image values behind the pair:

```{r colocplot, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 5}
plotMetricBoxplot(coloc, spe, "Activated Fibrotic FBs", "SMCs/Pericytes",
    "disease_status", metric = "lfunction")
```

::: callout-tip
## Many pairs, many tests

Every pair of cell types and groups is tested, so there are many tests, and groups overlap with their own subtypes. Look at `p.adj` (Benjamini-Hochberg) rather than `p.value`, and treat a pair that is only significant before adjustment as a lead to follow up, not a finding.
:::

# Niches

Niches are recurring local neighbourhoods: groups of cells that share a similar mix of surrounding cell types. `runNicheIdentification()` describes every cell by its local indicators of spatial association from lisaClust, at several radii, and clusters those profiles into `k` niches. It does this twice, with the hard labels and with the weights, in which each neighbour counts towards a cell type in proportion to its confidence.

```{r niches, results = "hide"}
niches = runNicheIdentification(spe, tree, confList, r = c(20, 50), k = 6)
```

How much do the weights change the niches? Each row below is a weighted niche, split by the unweighted niche its cells were in. Niche numbers are arbitrary, so look for the biggest entry in each row: a niche that keeps most of its cells has barely changed. Here almost every niche keeps most of its cells, so the weights change the niches very little.

```{r nichetable}
table(weighted = niches$nicheWeighted, unweighted = niches$nicheUnweighted)
```

Niche assignments are stored in the `colData` for the niche plots. `nicheCompositionMap()` shows which cell types are enriched in each niche:

```{r nichemap, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 6.5}
spe$nicheWeighted = niches$nicheWeighted[spe$cellID]
nicheCompositionMap(spe, "nicheWeighted")
```

and `plotNicheSpatial()` shows where a niche's cells are in an image:

```{r nichespatial, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 9}
plotNicheSpatial(spe, "VUHD038", "niche1")
```

The proportion of each niche can be tested against the outcome in the same way as the cell types:

```{r nichetest}
nicheTests = testNicheOutcome(spe, niches$nicheUnweighted,
    niches$nicheWeighted, outcomeCol = "disease_status", subject = "subject")
nicheTests$testWeighted
nicheTests$testUnweighted
```

`niche1`, which is rich in alveolar cells (AT1 and AT2 cells and capillaries) and macrophages, is less common in disease. The weighted and unweighted analyses agree here, as expected from how little the weights changed the niches.

# Practical notes

- **Use at least 100 bootstraps** (`nBoot`) for real analyses, and set `seed` so the confidences can be reproduced.
- **Large datasets:** `cores` runs the bootstrap on several cores, and `subprocess = TRUE` runs each group in a fresh R session, which keeps the workers small. The analysis functions take `cores` too.
- **An alternative to the bootstrap:** `crossfitLineageProbabilities()` returns cross-fitted class probabilities in the same format as `bootstrapLineageConfidence()`, so they can be used in exactly the same way.
- **Your own pipeline:** `confidenceWeights()` gives the cells-by-labels weight matrix for any function that takes `cellWeights`, such as `spicyR::spicy()` and `lisaClust::lisa()`.

# References

- Vannan et al. (2025). Xenium spatial transcriptomics of pulmonary fibrosis and control lung biopsies, available as `SpatialDatasets::spe_Vannan_2025()`; the subset used here is `lungSubset`.
- [spicyR](https://bioconductor.org/packages/spicyR): spatial linear and mixed-effects modelling of cell co-localisation.
- [lisaClust](https://bioconductor.org/packages/lisaClust): clustering of local indicators of spatial association.
- [Statial](https://bioconductor.org/packages/Statial): the Kontextual measure of relative co-localisation.
